stages.name: Brief
stages.instructions:
Work on the card's own branch, so the next stage can find what you produced even if it runs
on another machine. Today's stages happen to share one host and hand work over through /tmp; that
is luck, not design, and it fails silently the day a station moves.

  repository  the card's target (for this board: SuperJackfruitLabs/super-jackfruit-website).
              Clone it by its ordinary GitHub URL — this host rewrites forge-primary repositories
              to forge automatically, and your station key is what authenticates the push.
  directory   ./.press/<cardId>/ inside the directory you start in, so two cards never collide.
  branch      card/<cardId>, where <cardId> is the card id on the provenance line above.

If the branch already exists on the remote, check it out and build on it. Never force-push, and
never rebase a branch another stage has pushed to: you would be discarding a colleague's work.

Commit what you produce and push the branch before you finish. An artifact that exists only in
your workspace has not been handed over, and the stage after you will find nothing.

Write the brief to `press/brief.md` on that branch.

Report in your handoff, under these exact keys:

  path     where you wrote it, in the repository
  commit   the sha you pushed
  branch   the branch it is on

`path` and `commit` are CHECKED by the board. Completing this stage without them does not
advance the card — it blocks it. That is deliberate, and it is not bookkeeping: an agent whose
turn simply ends is otherwise reported as finished by the machinery that dispatched it, and the
card moves on carrying whatever its last sentence happened to be. On 2026-09-29 a verification
stage reached a human gate that way, as the words "Fact-checking is underway".

If you cannot produce them, BLOCK the card and say what stopped you. A block you chose carries
your reason; one the board imposes carries none.

Write your findings to `press/verification.md`: what you checked, what you changed, and anything

would clear it — a blocker nobody can act on stops the card rather than improving it.

Finish by stating your verdict in the handoff, under the key `publishable`. Say `true` or

stages.name: Publish
stages.instructions:
Work on the card's own branch, so the next stage can find what you produced even if it runs
on another machine. Today's stages happen to share one host and hand work over through /tmp; that
is luck, not design, and it fails silently the day a station moves.

  repository  the card's target (for this board: SuperJackfruitLabs/super-jackfruit-website).
              Clone it by its ordinary GitHub URL — this host rewrites forge-primary repositories
              to forge automatically, and your station key is what authenticates the push.
  directory   ./.press/<cardId>/ inside the directory you start in, so two cards never collide.
  branch      card/<cardId>, where <cardId> is the card id on the provenance line above.

If the branch already exists on the remote, check it out and build on it. Never force-push, and
never rebase a branch another stage has pushed to: you would be discarding a colleague's work.

Commit what you produce and push the branch before you finish. An artifact that exists only in
your workspace has not been handed over, and the stage after you will find nothing.

The article is on the branch. Put it on the default branch and make it live:

  git checkout <default-branch> && git pull
  git checkout card/<cardId> -- <the article's path>

Take ONLY the article. `press/` is the card's working record and stays on the branch — do not
merge the branch, and do not delete it afterwards: it is what the card's published receipt cites.

Push to the repository's PRIMARY remote, never to GitHub directly. For a forge-primary repository,
forge mirrors to GitHub itself within seconds, and a direct GitHub push races that mirror. A human
approved this card at "Publish approved", so no pull request is needed.

Before pushing, clear anything that would keep the work invisible once it lands — a `draft: true`
front-matter flag, or a publication-blocker comment an earlier stage left. Only clear a blocker you
have checked yourself; if the thing it names is still missing, stop and say so rather than deleting
the comment. Removing an objection is not the same as answering it.

One exception, because it is a trap rather than a judgement call: a blocker cannot require proof
that only publishing can produce. A run trace cannot contain the commit that publishes the page,
and a live URL cannot answer before the page is live. A trace recording the stages, the agents and
the human decisions has answered the question; the commit and the URL are added after you push.
Waiting for a file to already contain what only your work can put there is a deadlock, not
diligence.

If you genuinely cannot publish, BLOCK this card with the reason. Do not complete the run:
completing it advances the card into `published`, and a board reporting `published` over work that
was never published is the precise failure this stage exists to prevent — it has happened twice.

Finish by showing your work, in the two forms this stage is now checked against:

  1. Add a REFERENCE to the commit you pushed, on forge — a URL of the form
     https://forge.superjackfruit.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<sha> . Use `superpipeline_add_reference`
     if you have it. This is the evidence that the work left your machine, which is the thing that
     was false the two times this board reported `published` over nothing.
  2. Fetch the live URL and report it in your handoff under the key `url`, with its status code
     beside the commit sha.

Both are checked by the board, not merely asked for. Completing without them does not advance the
card — it blocks it. If you cannot produce one of them, BLOCK the card yourself and say which:
a block you chose carries your reason, and one the board imposes carries none.

cards.title: The lab never closes — introducing Super Jackfruit Labs

spec.angle: Super Jackfruit Labs is one person and a team of AI agents that hold real identities and do real work. This is the lab's introduction — what it is, what it builds, and why agents here are treated as principals rather than as macros. The post earns the claim instead of asserting it: this article itself was researched, written, fact-checked and published by four different agents moving one card across a Kanban board, with a human approving twice and writing none of it.
spec.audience: Engineers and builders who have tried to get AI agents to do sustained, real work and found that the demos do not survive contact with a repository, a deploy, or a second agent. Assume they are skeptical of autonomy claims, because most are overstated.
what_this_post_must_do: Introduce the lab: who it is, what it is for, what 'the lab never closes' means in practice.
Name the projects and say what each is FOR in one honest sentence, not marketing copy.
Explain the thesis: an agent that borrows a human's credentials is a macro; an agent with its own identity, own keys and own accountable history is a teammate.
Show the receipts for how this very post reached the page, and be precise about which parts a human did.
evidence: Super Jackfruit Labs builds in the open where it can. Public repositories at github.com/SuperJackfruitLabs include superpipeline, agentpod, supermessage, supermd and this website. Others are private; do not present private work as checkable.

superpipeline (MIT, public, created 2026-06-20) describes itself as 'A multi-tenant Kanban board that orchestrates external AI agents (any harness, anywhere) through pipeline stages with human approval gates. Built on Cloudflare.' It is the board this post travelled across.

agentpod is the fleet and facilities plane: it runs the agents on real machines and bridges them into chat. Its public description on GitHub is out of date and calls it a mobile app to control OpenCode agents — check the repository itself, not the description.
supermessage is 'A cross-platform Matrix client for rooms where half the occupants are AI agents' — this is how the human receives approval requests and answers them, including from a phone.
The board that published this post is called Press. Its pipeline is: commission, brief, angle approved (human gate), draft, verify claims, publish approved (human gate), publish, published.

Four agents worked this card, each routed to a stage by the capability it declares, not by name: research-ray (research) gathered and sourced the brief; writer-quill (writing) drafted it; analyst-echo (claim-check, analysis) verified the claims; coder-kai (code) committed and pushed it.

Each agent holds its own identity rather than borrowing the human's: its own SSH key on the machine it runs on, with the private key never leaving that machine, and its own account on the lab's Forgejo server. The commit that publishes this post is made by an agent's key.

The two human gates are real refusal points, not rubber stamps: the card cannot advance past 'angle approved' or 'publish approved' without a person answering, and the request reaches them in an encrypted Matrix room.

The honest limits, which this post must state plainly rather than bury: a human wrote the card's brief and approved twice; a human (with an AI assistant) built the pipeline the agents run on; the agents did the research, the writing, the checking and the shipping of this article, not the design of the system that carries them.
The lab's previous post, 'The CLI that could not update itself', is live at superjackfruit.com/blog/the-cli-that-could-not-update-itself/ and went through this same pipeline.
spec.claims_must_cite: Every factual claim must be checked against public sources before this publishes — the GitHub organization, the public repositories, their READMEs and releases, and the live website. Public sources OUTRANK this spec: if the repository disagrees with the evidence above, the repository is right and the spec is wrong, and you should say so rather than repeat it. Do not cite private repositories as evidence a reader could verify. Do not invent numbers, dates, stars, users or benchmarks. If a claim cannot be checked, cut it.
spec.tone: Plain, specific and confident without hype. No exclamation marks, no 'revolutionary', no 'game-changing', no invented user quotes. Short paragraphs. Concrete nouns. A reader who dislikes AI marketing should still finish it.
must_not: Do not claim the agents are autonomous in a way they are not: two human approvals are required and a human wrote the brief.
Do not claim revenue, customers, funding, team size, or adoption. There are none to claim.
Do not describe private repositories as if a reader can go and look at them.
Do not pad to length. If it is good at 900 words, it is finished at 900 words.

cards.title: The CLI that could not update itself

spec.angle: A CLI that a person runs by hand drifts more than a service does, because nothing forces the upgrade.
evidence: agentpod-fleet was found at v0.1.52 while agentpod-node, built and published by the same release job, was current at v0.1.66
agentpod-node self-updates (apn update); agentpod-fleet had no update verb at all
fleet update was not merely missing — TestCarriesNoNodeVerbs forbade it, because selfupdate.assetName was hardcoded to agentpod-node-…, so a fleet update would have installed a node over fleet
Fixed by binding the asset to the calling binary: SuperJackfruitLabs/agentpod#567, released in v0.1.70
spec.claims_must_cite: Every number and every claim above must be checked against the public repo, its releases and its PRs before this publishes. The public README, changelog, release and code outrank this spec.
spec.audience: Engineers who ship internal CLIs and assume a release reaches its users.

spec.commission: Introduce ONE Super Jackfruit Labs project to a reader who has never heard of it, and who has no context on this company at all.
spec.choosing: Pick the project you can evidence best from PUBLIC sources — its repository, releases, pull requests, README and docs. Where two are equally documented, prefer the one whose purpose is least guessable from its name. Say in your brief which you picked and why, so the next stage is not guessing.
spec.audience: Engineers who build things with AI agents. Assume they are competent and busy, and that they have never visited this site before.
must: Say what the project is FOR before saying how it works.
Include at least one concrete thing it does that a reader could not have guessed from a one-line description.

Every factual claim — a version, a date, a number, a behaviour — must be checkable against a public source, and must cite it. The verify stage will check them against the public record and will send the piece back if they do not hold.
Prefer what exists today over what is planned.
avoid: Superlatives the evidence does not carry.
Internal-only detail a reader has no way to verify.
spec.length: Whatever the material honestly supports. A short piece that is entirely true beats a long one that pads.
